the nuclear resonance fluorescence (NRF) of gamma radiation in Ir191 was investigated and that the absorption cross section for NRF was measured as a function of source and absorber temperatures between 90 K and 370 K.

(a) The resonance fluorescence cross section for 129 keV photons from the decay of 191 Os to 191 Ir has been measured as a function of temperature in the range 90–370 K. In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of resonance absorption of gamma rays in the 129 keV level of the nucleus of iridium 191.
the study of resonance absorption of 129 keV gamma-rays in Ir191.
the investigation of the resonance absorption of 129 keV gamma rays from Os191 in Ir191, the decay product of Os191.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the theory of Lamb on the resonant absorption of slow neutrons in crystals is applicable to the resonant absorption by gamma rays, and that the absorption cross-section is strongly dependent upon the frequency distribution of the vibrational spectrum of the solid at low temperatures.
the present theory of the nuclear magnetic moment of the proton is not yet satisfactory.
the theory of Lamb on neutron absorption in crystals is also valid for the case of nuclear gamma-ray absorption.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the absorption cross section of the gamma resonance in Ir191 can be explained by Lamb theory, if we use the correct phonon spectrum.
we have studied the resonance absorption of the 129 keV γ-ray from the decay of 191 Os in 191 Ir.
the absorption cross section for gamma resonance absorption in crystals at low temperatures depends strongly on the frequency distribution of the lattice vibrations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a single, high-quality, high-purity, single crystal of the target material is sufficient to achieve the required sensitivity.
we have demonstrated the feasibility of a new approach to the design of a gamma-ray detector.
we have shown the possibility to use the resonant absorption of gamma radiation to measure the temperature dependence of the phonon density of states of a crystal.
